title: Chapter 6 Quiz: Securing Your App with Spring Security
description: Test your knowledge of authentication, authorization, roles, and securing endpoints with Spring Security.

questions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
options: Authentication is about permissions, authorization is about identity
Authentication verifies identity, authorization determines access rights
Authentication is only for users, authorization is for roles
questions.explanation: Authentication confirms who you are; authorization decides what you can do.

questions.question: Adding spring‑boot‑starter‑security automatically secures all endpoints with a default username and a randomly generated password.
questions.explanation: Yes, Spring Boot's auto‑configuration secures all endpoints with HTTP Basic authentication and provides a default user with a generated password printed in the logs.

questions.question: The annotation used to enable method security with @PreAuthorize is _________.
questions.explanation: You need to add @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity(prePostEnabled = true) to enable @PreAuthorize annotations.

questions.question: Which class is used to configure in‑memory users?
questions.explanation: InMemoryUserDetailsManager is the implementation for storing user details in memory.

questions.question: The password encoder BCryptPasswordEncoder is a good choice for production applications.
questions.explanation: BCrypt is a strong, widely‑used password hashing algorithm and is recommended for production.

questions.question: Which method in HttpSecurity would you use to allow unauthenticated access to a specific URL?
questions.explanation: permitAll() grants access to everyone, including unauthenticated users.

questions.question: To enable form‑based login, you call _________ on HttpSecurity.
questions.explanation: formLogin() enables Spring Security's default login page and form processing.

questions.question: What does the @PreAuthorize annotation do?
options: It secures a method based on an expression before the method is executed
It encrypts the method's return value
questions.explanation: @PreAuthorize evaluates a security expression before the method is invoked; if false, AccessDeniedException is thrown.

questions.question: Spring Security automatically adds the prefix ROLE_ to roles defined with .roles() in UserDetails builder.
questions.explanation: Yes, .roles("USER") results in authority "ROLE_USER".

questions.question: What is the purpose of the {noop} prefix in a password?
options: It indicates no password encoding (plain text)
It tells Spring to use a no‑operation encoder
It means the password is null
questions.explanation: {noop} is a password encoder prefix that means 'no operation' – the password is stored in plain text. Use only for learning.

questions.question: The default logout URL provided by Spring Security is _________.
questions.explanation: By default, a POST to /logout logs out the user.

questions.question: Which of the following expressions would allow access to a method only for users with the role ADMIN?
questions.explanation: hasRole('ADMIN') checks for authority 'ROLE_ADMIN'; hasRole('ROLE_ADMIN') also works but is redundant.

questions.question: You can use @PreAuthorize on controller methods but not on service methods.
questions.explanation: @PreAuthorize works on any Spring bean method (controllers, services, repositories) as long as the proxy is invoked.

questions.question: What does CSRF stand for and why is it important?
options: Cross‑Site Request Forgery – it prevents malicious sites from performing actions on behalf of authenticated users
Client‑Side Request Forgery – it secures client‑side requests
Cross‑Site Scripting – it prevents script injection
Credential Security and Request Filtering – it validates credentials
questions.explanation: CSRF (Cross‑Site Request Forgery) is an attack that tricks a user into making unwanted requests. Spring Security enables CSRF protection by default for stateful apps.

questions.question: The method _________ in HttpSecurity allows you to specify a custom login page URL.
questions.explanation: loginPage() is used to set the URL of the custom login page.

questions.question: Which of the following is a recommended way to store passwords in a production Spring Boot application?
questions.explanation: BCryptPasswordEncoder is the recommended password encoder as it uses a strong, salted hashing algorithm.

questions.question: The .antMatchers() rules are evaluated from top to bottom, and the first match wins.
questions.explanation: Order matters; more specific rules should come before more general ones.

questions.question: What annotation is used to mark a configuration class for Spring Security?
questions.explanation: @EnableWebSecurity is used to enable Spring Security's web security support and provide a configuration class.

questions.question: The expression _________ in @PreAuthorize gives access to the currently authenticated principal.
questions.explanation: The authentication object is available in security expressions; you can get principal via authentication.principal.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the SecurityFilterChain bean?
options: It defines which filters are applied to which requests
questions.explanation: SecurityFilterChain is a list of security filters that are applied to requests matching a certain pattern; it is the core of Spring Security configuration.
